title: Wisdom asked, wealth given
sum: Solomon's reign begins with the whole nation on the move. The king leads all Israel's leaders to the high place at Gibeon, where Moses' tent of meeting and Bezalel's bronze altar still stand, and offers a thousand burnt offerings. That night God tells him to ask for anything. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to lead and judge this great people. God gives it, and adds riches, treasure and glory beyond any other king.

The chapter ends with a short list of Solomon's chariots, horsemen, silver, cedar and horse trade, copied almost word for word from 1 Kings 10. Placed here, it shows God's promise of wealth already coming true.
readings: Read beside Kings

1 Kings 3 tells the same dream, but with a different setting. There Solomon has married Pharaoh's daughter, the people sacrifice at high places, and Solomon worships at Gibeon "since the greatest high place was there" (1 Kings 3:4). Chronicles explains that Gibeon was the right place, because Moses' tent and altar were there (1:3–6). The judgment of the two mothers that follows in Kings is left out; Chronicles moves straight from the gift of wisdom to the gift of wealth.
Read as a pattern

The first scene of Solomon's reign sets the pattern for the whole book: the king gathers all Israel, seeks the LORD at the proper altar, and the LORD answers. Seeking (1:5) is Chronicles' key word for true worship, and here it leads to blessing at once.

views.H: Traditional readers take the scene as history: Solomon's first great public act was a national pilgrimage to the tabernacle at Gibeon, about 970 BC, and God's answer shaped his reign. The Talmud and later Jewish writers counted Solomon's wisdom as a real gift of God, seen in the books tradition gives him.
views.C: Critical scholars see the Chronicler correcting Kings. In Kings, worship at a high place is a problem; here it is legitimate because the tabernacle was there. The chapter's details about Bezalel's altar and the tent come from the Chronicler's own reading of 1 Chronicles 16:39 and 21:29, not from an older source.
views.S: Kings has Pharaoh's daughter, the people at the high places, the dream "in a dream at night," Solomon's longer speech in which he calls himself "only a youngster" (1 Kings 3:7), and the judgment of the two mothers. Chronicles has the whole assembly, Moses' tent and Bezalel's altar, a shorter prayer, and the wealth list moved up from 1 Kings 10:26–29.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition praised Solomon's request as the right choice: one who asks for wisdom receives everything with it. The midrash on Song of Songs compares Solomon to a royal adviser who asked for the king's daughter, knowing all the rest would come with her.
views.X: Christian readers connect Solomon's request with the promise that God gives wisdom to anyone who asks (James 1:5), and with Jesus' saying that those who seek God's kingdom first will have the rest given to them as well (Matthew 6:33).

deep.b: Chronicles is the only book that says Moses' tabernacle stood at Gibeon (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29; 2 Chronicles 1:3). When David brought the ark to Jerusalem, it went into a new tent there, while the old tent and its bronze altar stayed at Gibeon with Zadok and the priests. The ark and the altar were apart until Solomon's Temple brought them together (5:5). Traditional readers accept this as an old memory. Many critical scholars think the Chronicler worked it out to explain why a faithful king would worship at a high place, as 1 Kings 3:4 says Solomon did.

echoes: 1 Kings 3:4–15; 1 Kings 10:26–29; 1 Chronicles 16:39–40; 1 Chronicles 21:29–30; 1 Chronicles 29:23–25; Exodus 31:1–11; Exodus 38:1–7; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Proverbs 2:6; James 1:5; Matthew 6:33

settings.what: God's offer and Solomon's request at Gibeon
settings.when: After Solomon's thousand burnt offerings at the tabernacle in Gibeon, at the start of his reign
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 3:5–14, but Chronicles makes the setting a public act of worship by 'the whole assembly' at Moses' tent, and it leaves out the dream. Solomon asks for wisdom, 'for who can judge this great people of yours?', and God adds riches and glory. For the Chronicler's readers, Solomon's reign began by seeking God at the lawful altar. Wisdom to lead God's people is the first thing to ask for.

title: Cedar from Tyre
sum: Solomon makes up his mind to build, and counts out his workforce. He writes to Huram king of Tyre, the Hiram of Kings, asking for cedar, cypress and algum timber and for a master craftsman. His letter explains what the house is for: incense, the rows of bread, daily and festival offerings. And it admits that no house can hold the God whom the highest heavens cannot contain.

Huram answers with praise for the LORD, the maker of heaven and earth, and sends Huram-abi, a craftsman whose mother came from Dan. The timber will float down the coast to Joppa. Solomon counts the foreigners in the land and sets them to work.
readings: Read beside Kings

1 Kings 5 tells the same exchange more briefly and from Hiram's side: Hiram sends envoys first, and the deal is a trade agreement. In Chronicles Solomon writes first, and his letter becomes a short sermon on the Temple and on God's greatness. The craftsman, who appears only later in Kings (1 Kings 7:13–14), is part of the request from the start, so the builder of the Temple, like Bezalel of the tabernacle, is gifted by God.
Read as a new tabernacle

Many details recall the building of Moses' tent. Bezalel of Judah worked with Oholiab of the tribe of Dan (Exodus 31:1–6); now Solomon of Judah works with Huram-abi, son of a Danite woman. Both builders are filled with skill. Both lists of materials name gold, silver, bronze, purple, crimson and blue-violet.

views.H: Traditional readers take Solomon's treaty with Tyre as historical: Tyre had the timber, the skilled workers and the ships, and Israel had the grain and oil. Phoenician craftsmen are known to have worked across the region.
views.C: Critical scholars read Solomon's letter as the Chronicler's own composition, giving his theology of the Temple: a place of worship and of prayer, not a house that holds God. The forced labor of foreigners (2:17–18) replaces Kings' draft of Israelites (1 Kings 5:13), a change many see as deliberate.
views.S: In Kings Hiram's envoys come first, Solomon replies with a short request, and the labor force includes Israelites. In Chronicles Solomon writes unprompted and at length, the craftsman is requested at once, his mother is a Danite (Kings: a widow of Naphtali), and only foreigners are counted for forced labor. The wages are different too: Kings has yearly food for Hiram's palace; Chronicles has food for the woodcutters.
views.J: Rabbinic readers noted Hiram's praise of Israel's God and treated him as a righteous gentile for a time, though later legends made him a proud king who claimed to be a god (compare Ezekiel 28).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Hiram and the foreign workers a picture of the nations helping to build God's house, an idea Isaiah 60 develops and that the church applied to the gathering of the gentiles.

deep.b: Kings says Hiram the bronze worker was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali (1 Kings 7:14); Chronicles says his mother came "from the daughters of Dan" (2:14). Traditional harmonizers suggest she was born in Dan and married into Naphtali, or lived in the town of Dan, which lay in Naphtali's territory. Many critical scholars think Chronicles changed the tribe on purpose, to match Oholiab of Dan, Bezalel's partner (Exodus 31:6). The name Chronicles gives him, Huram-abi ("Huram my father" or "Huram is my father"), also has several explanations; see the note on 2:13.

echoes: 1 Kings 5:1–18; 1 Kings 7:13–14; Exodus 25–31; Exodus 31:1–6; 1 Chronicles 22:2–4; 1 Chronicles 29:1–9; Ezra 3:7; 1 Kings 8:27; Isaiah 66:1; Acts 7:48–50

settings.what: Solomon's letter to Huram king of Tyre
settings.when: As Solomon prepared to build the Temple
settings.why: Kings frames the request as the fulfilling of the promise to David (1 Kings 5:2–6). Chronicles adds what the house is for: incense, the bread of the Presence and the daily offerings, 'Israel's duty for all time.' It also adds that the heavens cannot hold God. For readers whose own Temple kept those same offerings, the letter said what the house was for and why it could never contain God.

settings.by: Huram king of Tyre, in a letter
settings.why: A foreign king blesses 'the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth,' and sends a skilled craftsman, Huram-abi, whose mother was of Dan. In Chronicles the craftsman echoes Oholiab of Dan, who built the tabernacle (Exodus 31:6), so the Temple repeats the tabernacle. Readers who rebuilt with cedar from Tyre and Sidon (Ezra 3:7) saw foreign help as part of God's plan.

title: On Mount Moriah
sum: The building begins in Solomon's fourth year, and Chronicles names the site for the first time in the Bible: Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David, at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. The rest of the chapter measures the house. A porch, a great hall lined with cypress and gold, precious stones, a most holy place covered with six hundred talents of gold, two great cherubim whose wings fill the room, and a curtain of blue-violet, purple and crimson.
Two bronze pillars stand at the front, named Jakin and Boaz.
readings: Read as a sacred map

Chronicles links three places in one sentence. Moriah is where Abraham was told to offer Isaac (Genesis 22:2). The threshing floor is where David's plague was stopped and fire fell on his altar (1 Chronicles 21). The Temple stands on the spot where God provided and where judgment was turned away. Many scholars think this link is the Chronicler's own; Jewish and Christian tradition accepted it, and it is now basic to how the Temple Mount is understood.
Read beside Kings

1 Kings 6–7 is much longer and full of building details. Chronicles shortens it, leaves out the side rooms, the palace buildings and the time it took, and adds the curtain (3:14), which Kings does not mention. Several numbers differ; see the variants on 3:4 and 3:15.

views.H: Traditional readers accept that the Temple was built on the hill where Abraham bound Isaac and where David built an altar, and that Chronicles preserves a true tradition. The measurements are taken as real, with the difficult numbers explained as different ways of measuring.
views.C: Critical scholars note that Genesis 22 speaks of "the land of Moriah," not a mountain, and that no older text identifies the Temple site with Abraham's mountain. The Chronicler joined them, and his measurements partly follow Kings and partly reflect later ideas, such as the height of the porch.
views.S: Kings dates the building to 480 years after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1); Chronicles gives only Solomon's fourth year and adds the site. Chronicles adds the curtain, the gold of Parvaim and the precious stones, makes the porch 120 cubits high and the pillars 35 cubits, and leaves out the side rooms and most of the carved woodwork.
views.J: Jewish tradition holds that the Temple stood where Isaac was bound and where Adam was created, and that its rock is the foundation stone of the world. The binding of Isaac (the Akedah) is read on Rosh Hashanah, and the merit of that offering is linked with the Temple's sacrifices.
views.X: Christian readers have long seen Moriah as a figure of Calvary: on the mountain where God provided a ram in Isaac's place, a greater sacrifice would one day be offered. The torn curtain at Jesus' death (Mark 15:38) recalls the curtain added here.

deep.b: The name Moriah appears only twice in the Bible: "the land of Moriah" in Genesis 22:2 and "Mount Moriah" here. Genesis also says Abraham named the place "The LORD Will See," and that people still said, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen" (Genesis 22:14), a saying many readers have heard as a hint of the Temple. 3:1 uses a form of the same verb: the LORD "had shown himself" (literally "was seen") to David. The Samaritans placed Abraham's mountain at Mount Gerizim instead. See the topic page on the Akedah.

echoes: 1 Kings 6:1–38; 1 Kings 7:15–22; Genesis 22:2; Genesis 22:14; 1 Chronicles 21:15–22:1; 1 Chronicles 28:11–19; Exodus 26:31–33; Jeremiah 52:21; Mark 15:38; Hebrews 9:3–8

title: Bronze and gold
sum: Chapter 4 lists the furnishings. In bronze: a great altar twenty cubits square, the Sea, a huge round tank on twelve oxen, ten basins, and the courtyard doors. In gold: ten lampstands, ten tables and a hundred bowls. Then comes a summary of Huram's bronze work, cast in clay in the Jordan valley, too heavy to weigh, and of Solomon's gold work for the inside of the house.
Most of the summary (4:11–5:1) is copied from 1 Kings 7:40–51, and the Plain English Translation uses the same English where the Hebrew is the same.
readings: Read as an inventory

Like the tabernacle chapters in Exodus, the list is meant to be read slowly. Every object has a place and a purpose: the altar for sacrifice, the Sea for the priests' washing, the basins for rinsing the offerings, the lamps and tables for the holy place. The point is that everything was made as it should be.
Read beside Kings

Chronicles adds the bronze altar (4:1), which Kings never describes, and gives the purposes of the basins and the Sea (4:6). It makes ten lampstands and ten tables where Kings has ten lampstands and one table. It has oxen where Kings has gourds under the Sea's rim, and 3,000 baths where Kings has 2,000.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the list as an accurate record. They explain the Sea's capacity as full volume versus usual filling, and the many tables as sitting beside the one table for the Presence Bread.
views.C: Critical scholars think 4:1 may once have stood in Kings and dropped out, or was written by the Chronicler to complete the list. Differences such as oxen for gourds are taken as copying errors in Chronicles' source or in Chronicles itself.
views.S: The bronze altar (4:1), the purposes in 4:6, the ten tables (4:8) and the priests' courtyard (4:9) are Chronicles' own. The capacity and the oxen differ from Kings (variants on 4:3 and 4:5). From 4:11 the two lists run side by side.
views.J: The rabbis worked out the Sea's dimensions and capacity in detail (Eruvin 14a–b), using the 3,000 baths of Chronicles and the 2,000 of Kings to discuss dry and liquid measure, and took its proportions as the rule that a circle is three times its width (Eruvin 14a); later commentators noted that this is not exact.
views.X: Christian writers have read the bronze Sea as a figure of baptism, where those who serve God are washed, and the lampstands as a figure of the church as the light of the world (Revelation 1:20).

deep.h: The Sea and the value of pi
deep.b: A Sea ten cubits across and thirty cubits around implies that the circle's circumference is three times its width. The Talmud takes this as a working rule (Eruvin 14a); later commentators noted that it rounds off pi. Several answers are given: the numbers are round figures; the width was measured from the outside of the lip and the circumference below it, inside the thickness of the metal (4:5 says a hand's breadth); or the curve of the lip made the two measurements differ. A later rabbinic reading, usually credited to the Vilna Gaon (18th century), notes that 1 Kings 7:23 spells "line" with an extra letter, and the letters' values give a ratio close to pi. That reading is a curiosity, not a calculation the writer intended.

echoes: 1 Kings 7:23–51; Exodus 27:1–8; Exodus 30:17–21; Exodus 25:23–40; Exodus 37–38; 1 Chronicles 28:14–18; Jeremiah 52:17–23; Revelation 1:12–20; Revelation 4:6

title: The cloud fills the house
sum: With the work complete, Solomon stores David's gifts in the treasuries and calls Israel's leaders to Jerusalem at the feast of the seventh month. The Levites lift the ark and carry it, with the tent of meeting, up to the Temple. Sacrifices are beyond counting. The priests set the ark in the most holy place under the cherubim's wings; it holds only the two tablets of the covenant.

As the priests come out, a great choir of Levites in linen, with cymbals, harps and lyres, and a hundred and twenty priests with trumpets make one sound in praise: "For he is good, for his loyal love is forever." Then a cloud fills the house, and the priests cannot stay to serve.
readings: Read beside Kings

The story follows 1 Kings 8:1–11 closely. Chronicles makes the Levites, not the priests, lift the ark (5:4), as David had ordered (1 Chronicles 15:2), and adds 5:11–13: the singers, the trumpets and the praise. In Kings, the cloud fills the house when the priests come out. In Chronicles, it comes when the music begins.
Read as worship

For Chronicles the climax of the ark's journey is not only that it arrives but that God is praised. David had organized the singers and their song (1 Chronicles 16:34, 41). Now that song is sung in the Temple, and God answers with his glory. Music is not decoration but part of how the house becomes God's house.

views.H: Traditional readers take the scene as a historical event soon after the building was finished (1 Kings 6:38), during the Feast of Booths, when God showed his presence in the cloud as he had done at the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35).
views.C: Critical scholars see the added verses about the Levitical singers as reflecting the worship of the Second Temple, when the singers were a prominent order. The Chronicler places his own day's worship at the Temple's founding.
views.S: Chronicles follows Kings almost word for word, except that the Levites lift the ark (5:4), the Levite priests carry it (5:5; see the variant), and 5:11b–13a is new. Kings' Hebrew has the month name Ethanim; Chronicles does not.
views.J: "For he is good, for his loyal love is forever" became a central line of Jewish prayer, said in the Hallel on festivals (Psalm 118; Psalm 136). The Talmud pictures the ark's poles pressing against the curtain so that they could be seen from the holy place without showing outside (Yoma 54a; compare 5:9).
views.X: Christian readers connect the cloud of glory with the Spirit filling the house where the disciples met at Pentecost (Acts 2:1–4) and with the Word who "lived among us" (John 1:14), as God's presence once lived in the Temple.

deep.b: 5:13 stresses unity: the trumpeters and singers are "as one," "making one sound heard." The Levites stand at the east of the altar with the families David set up, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 25), and with them a hundred and twenty priests, perhaps five for each of the twenty-four priestly divisions. All the divisions serve together (5:11), not in their usual turns. Chronicles pictures the whole of Israel's worship gathered into one moment, and God's glory comes in answer.

echoes: 1 Kings 8:1–11; Exodus 40:34–35; 1 Chronicles 15:2; 1 Chronicles 16:4–6; 1 Chronicles 16:34; 1 Chronicles 25:1–7; Psalm 118:1; Psalm 136:1; Ezra 3:10–11; Ezekiel 10:3–4; Ezekiel 43:4–5; Acts 2:1–4

settings.what: The song at the ark's coming
settings.by: The Levite singers and the priests with trumpets, 'as one'
settings.to: The LORD, before all Israel at the dedication
settings.when: As the priests came out of the holy place, in the seventh month
settings.why: 'For he is good, for his loyal love is forever.' The cloud fills the house as soon as the song is raised. Chronicles adds the singers to the scene in 1 Kings 8:10–11, so that the glory comes at the moment of Levitical praise. The refrain was sung in the readers' own Temple (Ezra 3:11), and the scene gave it great authority.

title: A house of prayer
sum: Solomon blesses the assembly and tells the story of the house: God chose no city and no man until he chose Jerusalem and David. David wanted to build, but it was for his son to do. Then, from a bronze platform in the courtyard, Solomon kneels and prays the longest prayer in the book.

He asks God, whom the highest heavens cannot hold, to listen to every prayer offered toward this house: in a lawsuit, after defeat, in drought, famine or plague, when a foreigner comes, when the army goes out, and even when Israel is taken as prisoners to a far land. Each time the answer he asks for is the same: hear from the heavens, and forgive. The prayer ends with lines from Psalm 132, calling the LORD to rise to his place of rest.
readings: Read beside Kings

Most of the prayer follows 1 Kings 8:12–50 word for word. Chronicles adds the bronze platform (6:13), shortens the end, and replaces Kings' closing appeal to the exodus (1 Kings 8:51–53) with Psalm 132, an appeal to God's promise to David. Its prayer looks to the covenant with David rather than to Moses.
Read for the exiles

The seventh request (6:36–39) imagines Israel captive in a foreign land, turning back and praying toward Jerusalem. For the Chronicler's readers, after the exile, that had happened. The prayer gave them words, and the promise of 7:14 answered it.

views.H: Traditional readers take the prayer as Solomon's own, spoken at the dedication about 960 BC, with prophetic foresight about exile drawn from Moses' warnings (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28).
views.C: Most critical scholars think the prayer in Kings was shaped by writers during the exile, who knew the fall of Jerusalem. The Chronicler took it over and changed its ending to point to David and the hope of a restored kingdom.
views.S: 6:5b–6a, absent from Kings, completes the balance of the sentence (see the variants); 6:13 adds the platform; 6:16 has "walk in my law" where Kings has "walk before me"; 6:40–42 replaces 1 Kings 8:50b–53 with Psalm 132:8–10.
views.J: Jewish prayer is directed toward Jerusalem because of this chapter: those outside the land face the land, those in the land face Jerusalem, and those in Jerusalem face the Temple (Berakhot 30a, citing Solomon's prayer). Daniel prays toward Jerusalem from Babylon (Daniel 6:10).
views.X: Jesus quoted Isaiah's phrase "a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7) when he cleared the Temple, a hope already present in Solomon's request for the foreigner (6:32–33). Christians have read the prayer's question, whether God can live on earth (6:18), as answered in the incarnation.

deep.b: Solomon's requests fall into seven cases: (1) a dispute between neighbors, settled by an oath at the altar (6:22–23); (2) defeat in war (6:24–25); (3) drought (6:26–27); (4) famine, disease, locusts or siege (6:28–31); (5) the prayer of a foreigner (6:32–33); (6) Israel's army in the field (6:34–35); (7) exile (6:36–39). Each case follows the same form: if this happens, and they pray toward this place, then hear from the heavens and act. The repeated "from the heavens" keeps both truths together: God's name is in the house, but God himself lives in heaven (6:18; 6:21).

6:41–42 adapts Psalm 132:8–10, a pilgrim song that remembers David's search for a home for the ark. Chronicles changes the psalm in small ways: it adds "And now" and "God," and uses a shorter word for "place of rest"; the priests "wear salvation" (the psalm has "righteousness" in its verse 9, "salvation" in verse 16); and "your faithful ones" are "glad in good things." The psalm's "for the sake of David your servant" becomes the final line, "Remember the loyal love shown to David your servant," which may echo Isaiah 55:3. Psalms is not yet on this site, so the lines are freshly translated from Chronicles' Hebrew.

echoes: 1 Kings 8:12–53; Psalm 132:1–10; Exodus 40:34–38; Leviticus 26:40–45; Deuteronomy 4:29–31; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Isaiah 55:3; Isaiah 56:7; Daniel 6:10; Daniel 9:4–19; Nehemiah 1:5–11; Mark 11:17; John 4:20–24; Acts 7:47–50

settings.what: Solomon's words and blessing of the assembly
settings.to: The LORD (6:1–2); then all the assembly of Israel, standing
settings.when: At the dedication of the Temple, after the cloud filled the house
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 8:12–21. Solomon tells how God chose Jerusalem and David, how David wished to build, and how God kept his word. In Kings the speech marks the high point of the monarchy for exiles who had lost it. In Chronicles it tells readers in a rebuilt Temple that the choice of Jerusalem and of David still stands.

settings.by: Solomon, kneeling on a bronze platform with palms raised
settings.to: The LORD, God of Israel, before all the assembly of Israel
settings.when: At the dedication of the Temple, about 960 BC
settings.why: The same prayer as 1 Kings 8:22–53. It sets out seven cases in which God is asked to hear prayer toward this house and forgive: oaths, defeat, drought, plague, the foreigner, war and exile. In Kings the prayer gives exiles words to repent in a far land. Chronicles ends it not with the exodus (1 Kings 8:51–53) but with Psalm 132 and the promise to David. For its readers, back in the land with a Temple again, the prayer has been answered. Their hope is tied to David's house.

title: If my people humble themselves
sum: When Solomon finishes praying, fire falls from heaven onto the sacrifices and the LORD's glory fills the house. All Israel kneels on the pavement and sings the refrain of praise. The dedication lasts seven days, followed by seven days of the feast, with gatherings from the far north to the border of Egypt.

Later the LORD appears to Solomon at night with an answer. When he sends drought, locusts or plague, if his people humble themselves, pray, seek his face and turn from their evil, he will hear, forgive and heal their land. If Solomon walks as David did, his throne will stand. But if they turn to other gods, God will pull them up from the land and make this house an object of shock.
readings: Read as God's answer

7:13–15 answers Solomon's prayer case by case, using its own words: the sky locked shut (6:26), locusts and disease (6:28), and open eyes and attentive ears (6:40). 7:14, which Kings does not have, gathers the whole prayer into four verbs: humble, pray, seek, turn. It becomes the key to the rest of the book.
Read beside Kings

Kings has no fire from heaven; the glory comes in 1 Kings 8:10–11 only. Chronicles adds the fire (7:1–3), as at the tabernacle (Leviticus 9:24) and at David's altar (1 Chronicles 21:26). It changes the dates so that the feast ends on the twenty-third day (7:10), and it adds 7:12b–15 to God's reply.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the fire as a miracle like those at Sinai's tabernacle and at Elijah's altar (1 Kings 18:38), marking God's acceptance of the Temple.
views.C: Critical scholars see the fire as the Chronicler's way of making the Temple the true successor of the tabernacle and of David's altar on Ornan's threshing floor. 7:14 sums up his theology of repentance, which shapes his retelling of almost every later king.
views.S: 7:1–3 and 7:12b–15 are Chronicles' own. 7:4–10 follows 1 Kings 8:62–66 with changes of order and dates. 7:11–22 follows 1 Kings 9:1–9, with small changes such as "ruling over Israel" (7:18) for Kings' "from Israel's throne."
views.J: The Talmud counts the fire from heaven among five things that Solomon's Temple had and the Second Temple lacked, with the ark, the divine presence, the holy spirit and the Urim and Thummim (Yoma 21b). 7:14 is used in Jewish teaching on repentance (teshuvah) as the path back to God for a whole people.
views.X: 7:14 is one of the most quoted verses of the Old Testament among Christians, especially in calls to national prayer. Many teachers warn that it was addressed to Israel and its land; others apply it, by analogy, to the church.

deep.b: The verse names a people "over whom my name has been called," meaning God's own people, and a land that God promised to heal. In Chronicles it becomes the pattern for every later king: Rehoboam humbles himself and is spared (12:6–7; 12:12), Asa seeks God and has rest, Manasseh humbles himself in exile and is restored (33:12–13). Modern readers often apply it to their own nations. Scholars and pastors debate whether that is a fair use. Many say the verse's promise of a healed land belongs to Israel's covenant, while its call to humble prayer applies to all God's people.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a prayer and its answer as the book's table of contents
deep.b: My own reading: 6:22–39 and 7:13–15 work as a table of contents for the rest of 2 Chronicles. Many of the later crises fit one of Solomon's cases: defeat before an enemy (Ahaz, 28:5), war fought with prayer (Abijah, 13:14; Jehoshaphat, 20:5–12), prayer in captivity (Manasseh, 33:12–13), a foreign king who honors the God of the house (Cyrus, 36:22–23), and at the end, exile and return (36:20–23). Scholars have long noted the importance of 7:14; reading the prayer's seven cases as an outline that the Chronicler fills in, king by king, is my own suggestion.

echoes: 1 Kings 8:54–66; 1 Kings 9:1–9; Leviticus 9:23–24; 1 Chronicles 21:26; 1 Kings 18:38; Deuteronomy 28:37; Deuteronomy 29:24–28; Jeremiah 22:8–9; Psalm 136; 2 Chronicles 33:12–13; James 4:10

settings.by: All the Israelites, kneeling on the pavement
settings.when: When fire came down and the glory filled the house
settings.why: The whole people take up the Levites' refrain: 'For he is good, for his loyal love is forever.' The fire from heaven, added by Chronicles, echoes the first sacrifice at the tabernacle (Leviticus 9:24) and David's altar (1 Chronicles 21:26). For readers it marked their Temple's site and worship as approved by God.

settings.when: After the dedication and the building of the palace
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 9:1–9, but Chronicles adds 7:13–15. If my people humble themselves, pray, seek my face and turn back, I will hear, forgive and heal their land. In Kings the warning of a ruined house explains the exile. In Chronicles the added promise is the key to the whole book, and it was meant for readers who had come through the ruin: the way back is always open.

title: Solomon's works
sum: After twenty years of building, Solomon turns to the rest of his kingdom. He rebuilds towns Huram gave him, takes Hamath-zobah in Syria, builds Tadmor in the desert, Upper and Lower Beth-horon, and storage and chariot towns. The peoples left from the old Canaanite nations become his work gangs; the Israelites are his soldiers and officers.

He moves Pharaoh's daughter out of David's city because the ark has made it holy. He offers sacrifices by the calendar of Moses and sets the priests, Levites and gatekeepers in their places by David's order. Then he sends ships with Huram's sailors from Eloth to Ophir, and they bring back 450 talents of gold.
readings: Read beside Kings

Kings says Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in Galilee, which Hiram disliked (1 Kings 9:11–13). Chronicles says the towns Huram gave Solomon, Solomon rebuilt (8:2). Kings mentions Pharaoh's daughter as Solomon's wife at the start of his reign; Chronicles mentions her only here, and only to keep her out of a holy place. Chronicles adds the war at Hamath-zobah and the details of worship (8:13–15).
Read as completion

8:16 sums up everything: Solomon's work was in order from foundation to finish, "The LORD's house was complete." The chapter's real interest is not towns and ships but the Temple's daily life, which goes on exactly as Moses and David commanded.

views.H: Traditional readers harmonize the towns: Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns as security, Hiram returned them, and Solomon rebuilt them. Tadmor (later Palmyra) is taken as a real outpost on the desert trade route.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the Chronicler reworked Kings to avoid Israel giving away its land. Some read Tadmor as a misreading of Tamar (1 Kings 9:18, in the Judean wilderness), and the war at Hamath-zobah as unhistorical.
views.S: Kings' twenty towns given to Hiram (1 Kings 9:10–14) become towns received from Hiram. Kings' Gezer story (1 Kings 9:15–17) is gone. The Ketiv of Kings' "Tamar" (Tadmor in the Qere) becomes Tadmor in Chronicles. 8:13–15 is new. The figures for officers (8:10) and gold (8:18) differ; see the variants.
views.J: Rabbinic readers took 8:11 as evidence of Solomon's piety: he would not let a foreign wife live where the ark had been. Others noted that he married her at all, and the Talmud says that on the day he married her, Gabriel planted a reed in the sea on which Rome would one day be built (Shabbat 56b).
views.X: Christian readers have often passed quickly over this chapter, though some note the parallel between a house set in order and Paul's call for worship to be done properly and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

deep.b: Tadmor is the old name of Palmyra, an oasis in the Syrian desert on the caravan road between Damascus and the Euphrates. 1 Kings 9:18 has a written form (Ketiv) that reads Tamar, a place in the Judean wilderness south of the Dead Sea, while its reading tradition (Qere) has Tadmor. Many scholars think Kings originally meant Tamar and that Chronicles, or the readers of Kings, understood it as the far more famous Tadmor. Traditional readers hold that Solomon's control of trade routes could have reached Palmyra, given his campaign at Hamath (8:3–4).

echoes: 1 Kings 9:10–28; 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 7:8; Numbers 28–29; Deuteronomy 16:16; 1 Chronicles 23–26; 1 Kings 22:48; Ezra 3:4–5

settings.to: His household; reported for the readers
settings.when: When he moved Pharaoh's daughter to her own house
settings.why: 'No wife of mine will live in the house of David... because the places the LORD's ark has come into are holy.' Chronicles leaves out Solomon's many foreign wives (1 Kings 11:1–8). Pharaoh's daughter is the only one it shows living with him, and it gives a reason of holiness for keeping her apart. The concern is the holiness of the place where the ark had been. For readers, whose own Temple was guarded from anything unclean, it showed holiness guarding the holy place.

settings.to: The priests in their divisions, the Levites, and the gatekeepers
settings.why: Offerings are made as Moses commanded on Sabbaths, new moons and the three feasts, and the clergy serve by the divisions David set. The passage binds the Temple staff to both authorities, Moses for the sacrifices and David for the music and the order. That was exactly how the readers' Temple was run.

title: The queen and the gold
sum: The queen of Sheba comes from southern Arabia to test Solomon's wisdom. He answers every question. She sees his house, his table and his servants, and it takes her breath away. She praises the LORD, who put Solomon on his own throne, and gives him gold, spices and gems. Then she goes home.

Solomon's wealth is measured: 666 talents of gold a year, gold shields, an ivory throne with lions, gold cups, ships to Tarshish, gifts from every king, horses and chariots. Then the account of his reign closes. He reigned forty years, and Rehoboam became king.
readings: Read beside Kings

Chapter 9 follows 1 Kings 10 almost word for word, with the Plain English Translation using the site's wording of Kings wherever the Hebrew matches. The real difference is what comes after. Kings follows Solomon's glory with his many foreign wives, his idols, God's anger and the rebels God raised against him (1 Kings 11). Chronicles goes straight from glory to his death.
Read as fulfillment

The chapter fulfills 1:12: God promised wisdom, and the queen tests and confirms it; he promised wealth and glory beyond any king, and 9:22 says it came true. The book has shown God keeping his word to Solomon from start to finish.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the visit and the wealth as history, and explain the omission of Solomon's sins by the Chronicler's purpose: he wrote for readers who knew Kings, and he chose what served his message.
views.C: Critical scholars see an idealized Solomon. Chronicles presents David and Solomon as one golden age, and silence about Solomon's sin is part of that picture. The figures of gold are taken as legendary.
views.S: 9:1–28 is a close copy of 1 Kings 10:1–28, with small changes: "on his own throne" (9:8), the stairway (9:4), the footstool (9:18), "going to Tarshish" (9:21), and 9:26 added from 1 Kings 4:21. 1 Kings 11:1–40 is left out. 9:29–31 follows 1 Kings 11:41–43, but names prophets' records instead of "the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds."
views.J: Jewish tradition debated Solomon's guilt. The Talmud records the view that whoever says Solomon sinned is mistaken, reading 1 Kings 11 as his failure to restrain his wives, alongside sharper judgments (Shabbat 56b). The queen became the subject of many legends, as the 1 Kings 10 page shows.
views.X: Jesus pointed to the queen of the south, who came from far away to hear Solomon's wisdom, and said that someone greater than Solomon was there (Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31).

deep.h: Why Chronicles leaves out Solomon's sins
deep.b: 1 Kings 11 tells of Solomon's seven hundred wives, his worship of other gods, and God's judgment. Chronicles says nothing of it, and readers have explained this in several ways. An ideal reign: many critical scholars (Japhet, Williamson) think the Chronicler presents David and Solomon as one ideal reign, the model for the Temple and its worship, and a model is not spoiled. Assumed knowledge: traditional readers point out that Chronicles also leaves out much good in Kings; it assumes its readers know the earlier book (see 10:15, which presupposes Ahijah's prophecy in 1 Kings 11). Not entirely silent: Chronicles does mention the hard service Solomon laid on the people (10:4), and Nehemiah 13:26 knew of his foreign wives. The theology of the book: since Chronicles links sin and punishment within a lifetime, telling Solomon's sin would have required telling his punishment; leaving both out keeps the focus on the Temple. Most scholars see more than one of these reasons at work.

echoes: 1 Kings 10:1–29; 1 Kings 11:41–43; 1 Kings 4:21; 1:12; 1 Kings 11:1–40; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Psalm 72:10–15; Isaiah 60:6; Nehemiah 13:26; Matthew 6:29; Matthew 12:42; Luke 11:31

settings.when: After she tested his wisdom and saw his house
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 10:6–9, but Chronicles has her say God set Solomon 'on his own throne, as king for the LORD your God.' A foreign queen confesses that Israel's king rules on God's behalf. For readers it said that the kingdom was always God's, and that the nations would see it.

title: The kingdom splits
sum: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king. Jeroboam, back from exile in Egypt, leads all Israel in a request: lighten the heavy yoke Solomon put on them. The old advisers say to be kind and speak good words. The young men Rehoboam grew up with tell him to boast and threaten. He takes their advice: "My father punished you with whips, but I with scorpions."
The northern tribes answer, "What is our share in David?" and go home. They stone Rehoboam's labor boss, and the king flees to Jerusalem. Israel has broken away from the house of David.
readings: Read beside Kings

The chapter is nearly identical to 1 Kings 12:1–19. Chronicles keeps 10:15, which mentions Ahijah's word to Jeroboam, though it never told that prophecy (1 Kings 11:29–39). It leaves out the next part of Kings: Jeroboam made king of Israel and his golden calves (1 Kings 12:20–33), because from here on it follows only Judah.
Read as God's turn

Rehoboam makes a foolish choice, but 10:15 says "God had brought about this turn." The split is both a human failure and God's judgment. Chronicles never denies that the northern tribes are part of Israel, and it will keep calling them back (11:16; 30:6).

views.H: Traditional readers accept the account as history, about 930 BC, and read it as both the result of Solomon's taxes and labor and the fulfillment of Ahijah's prophecy.
views.C: Critical scholars see the account as shaped in the south, but recognize old tensions between north and south behind it. The Chronicler copied Kings because it shows the north leaving David, not the other way around.
views.S: Chronicles follows 1 Kings 12:1–19 closely, with small differences: Jeroboam "came back from Egypt" (10:2), the elders' advice "Be kind" (10:7), and the boys' message (10:14; see the variant). It does not have 1 Kings 12:20.
views.J: The rabbis taught that the split happened because Solomon taxed the people heavily and because Rehoboam listened to the young. A saying in the Talmud warns that the building of the young is destruction, and the destruction of the old is building (Nedarim 40a).
views.X: Christian readers have used Rehoboam's choice as a lesson in leadership: the one who serves the people will be served by them. Some connect the elders' advice in 1 Kings 12:7 with Jesus' words that the greatest must be the servant of all (Mark 10:43–44).

echoes: 1 Kings 12:1–19; 1 Kings 11:26–40; 1 Kings 4:6; 1 Kings 5:13–14; 2 Samuel 20:1; 1 Chronicles 5:1–2; 2 Chronicles 13:4–12; 2 Chronicles 30:6–9; Mark 10:42–45

settings.what: The people's request and Rehoboam's hard answer
settings.by: Jeroboam and all Israel; the elders; the young men; Rehoboam
settings.to: Rehoboam at Shechem; then the people
settings.when: At Rehoboam's coronation at Shechem, about 930 BC
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 12:1–15, copied almost unchanged. The people ask for a lighter yoke; the elders advise kindness; the young men advise harshness, and Rehoboam threatens 'scorpions.' Both books say God brought it about to keep his word to Jeroboam (10:15; 1 Kings 12:15). The difference lies around the scene. Chronicles leaves out Jeroboam's crowning over Israel (1 Kings 12:20) and the north's later history, so the split is told only as Judah's loss. Abijah (13:4–12) and Hezekiah (30:6–9) later treat it as a breach to be healed. Readers learn that harsh rule drives God's people apart.

settings.to: Rehoboam and the house of David
settings.why: 'What is our share in David?... Every man to your tents, Israel!' The old rebel cry (2 Samuel 20:1) ends the united kingdom. For readers who still hoped for all Israel around David's house, it named the break that Abijah (13:4–12) and Hezekiah (30:6–9) later try to heal.

title: Rehoboam's three good years
sum: Rehoboam raises an army to win back the north, but the prophet Shemaiah tells them not to fight their brothers, and they obey. Rehoboam fortifies fifteen towns around Judah. The priests and Levites of the north, thrown out by Jeroboam, come south, and with them come people from every tribe who want to seek the LORD. For three years Judah walks in the way of David and Solomon and grows strong.

The chapter closes with Rehoboam's family: eighteen wives, sixty concubines, twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters. He favors Maacah, Absalom's daughter, and names her son Abijah as heir, while he spreads the other sons through the fortified towns.
readings: Read as a pattern

Rehoboam's reign shows the pattern Chronicles will use for many kings. Obedience (11:4) brings strength (11:5–12), faithful worship brings people back (11:13–17), and wealth and family follow as signs of blessing (11:18–23). Then, in chapter 12, comes the turn: once strong, he leaves the LORD.
Read beside Kings

Only 11:1–4 has a parallel in Kings (1 Kings 12:21–24). The list of fortresses, the coming of the Levites and Rehoboam's family are Chronicles' own. Kings tells that Jeroboam made priests of non-Levites (1 Kings 12:31); Chronicles tells what happened to the Levites he replaced.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the list of fortresses and the family as drawn from Judah's records. The faithful from the north are taken as real migrants who chose Jerusalem over Jeroboam's shrines.
views.C: Critical scholars debate the fortresses. Some date the list to Rehoboam, after Shishak's invasion; others to Hezekiah or Josiah, when Judah's defenses were organized against Assyria. The coming of the faithful from the north is seen as the Chronicler's picture of "all Israel" gathering around Jerusalem.
views.S: 11:1–4 follows 1 Kings 12:21–24 with small changes: "all Israel in Judah and Benjamin" (11:3) and "they turned back from going against Jeroboam" (11:4). 11:5–23 has no parallel. Kings mentions Maacah only as Abijam's mother (1 Kings 15:2).
views.J: Rabbinic readers noted that Shemaiah stopped a civil war and praised the people for listening to a prophet. Jeroboam's priests became a byword for unfit priests.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the faithful who left the north "to seek the LORD" a picture of believers who leave comfort and home to worship God truly, and in Shemaiah's command an example of a peace made by obedience.

deep.b: The fifteen towns of 11:6–10 form a ring around the heart of Judah: Bethlehem, Etam and Tekoa to the east and south of Jerusalem; Beth-zur, Hebron and Ziph in the south; Adoraim, Lachish, Mareshah, Gath and Soco on the western slopes; and Azekah, Adullam, Zorah and Aijalon toward the Shephelah. The north is left open, perhaps because Rehoboam still hoped to win back Israel, or because the border there was guarded by Jerusalem itself. Archaeologists have dated building work at several of these sites, but scholars disagree whether the list belongs to Rehoboam's time or a later king's. See the note on 11:5.

echoes: 1 Kings 12:21–24; 1 Kings 12:25–33; 1 Kings 13:33–34; 1 Kings 14:21; 1 Kings 15:2; 2 Samuel 14:27; 2 Chronicles 13:9; 2 Chronicles 15:9; 2 Chronicles 30:11

settings.by: Shemaiah the man of God, for the LORD
settings.to: Rehoboam king of Judah and 'all Israel in Judah and Benjamin'
settings.when: When Rehoboam gathered 180,000 men to fight the north
settings.why: 'You must not march up and fight with your kinsmen.' The same scene as 1 Kings 12:22–24. Chronicles keeps the word 'kinsmen' and calls the people of the south 'all Israel,' so readers hear that the northerners were still brothers, even when their kingdom was wrong.

title: Shishak and Shemaiah
sum: Once his kingdom is strong, Rehoboam leaves the LORD's law, and all Israel with him. In his fifth year Shishak of Egypt invades with chariots, horsemen and troops from Libya and Cush, takes Judah's fortified towns and reaches Jerusalem. Shemaiah tells the leaders that because they left the LORD, he has left them to Shishak. They humble themselves: "The LORD is in the right."

God spares them from destruction but lets them serve Shishak, to learn the difference between serving him and serving foreign kings. Shishak takes the Temple's and the palace's treasures, including Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze. Rehoboam reigns seventeen years, does evil and dies.
readings: Read beside Kings

1 Kings 14:21–31 gives Shishak's invasion in a few lines and Rehoboam's reign as a time when Judah built high places and standing stones. Chronicles adds the size of Shishak's army, the capture of the fortified towns, Shemaiah's warning and the people's humbling. Its explanation is clear: the invasion was the result of their unfaithfulness, and the rescue the result of their humbling.
Read as 7:14 in action

The chapter is the first test of God's promise in 7:14. The people sin, God sends trouble, they humble themselves, and God limits the punishment. But they still serve Egypt, and the gold is gone. Humbling saves them from destruction, not from all loss.

views.H: Traditional readers accept Shishak's invasion as history, confirmed by the Egyptian record at Karnak, and Shemaiah's preaching as the reason the city was spared.
views.C: Critical scholars accept the invasion, which Shoshenq I's relief at Karnak confirms, but note that Shoshenq's list concentrates on the Negev and the northern kingdom and does not clearly mention Jerusalem. The pattern of sin, punishment, humbling and rescue is the Chronicler's own explanation.
views.S: Kings blames Judah's high places and shrine men (1 Kings 14:22–24) and simply records the attack (14:25–26). Chronicles adds 12:2b–8 and 12:12, and gives the Kings verdict in its own words: "He had not made his heart ready to seek the LORD" (12:14).
views.J: The Talmud tells that the treasure Joseph gathered in Egypt went out with Israel at the exodus and stayed in Jerusalem until Shishak took it back from Rehoboam (Pesachim 119a).
views.X: Christian readers have found in 12:8 a lesson that serving God is freedom compared with serving other masters, an idea close to Jesus' words that his yoke is easy (Matthew 11:28–30).

deep.b: Shoshenq I, founder of Egypt's 22nd dynasty, recorded his campaign on the wall of the temple of Amun at Karnak, beside the Bubastite Portal. The relief lists about 150 places, many in the Negev and in the northern kingdom, including Megiddo, where a piece of his victory stele was found. Jerusalem does not appear in the surviving list, though parts of it are damaged. Some scholars think Rehoboam paid Shishak off, which would explain why the city is missing and why 12:9 speaks of treasure rather than conquest. Others think the campaign was aimed mainly at Israel and the trade routes. See the topic page on Shishak.

echoes: 1 Kings 14:21–31; 1 Kings 11:40; 7:14; 1 Kings 10:16–17; 9:15–16; Leviticus 26:40–42; Deuteronomy 28:47–48; Nehemiah 9:36–37; Matthew 11:28–30

settings.what: Shemaiah's oracle and the leaders' confession
settings.by: Shemaiah the prophet; then the king and the leaders; then the LORD to Shemaiah
settings.to: Rehoboam and Judah's leaders gathered in Jerusalem
settings.when: During Shishak of Egypt's invasion, Rehoboam's fifth year, about 925 BC
settings.why: 'You have left me, so I in turn have left you.' The leaders humble themselves ('The LORD is in the right'). God gives 'a little escape' but makes them Shishak's servants. 'Then they will know what it is to serve me, and what it is to serve the kingdoms of the lands.' This is the first test of 7:14. For readers serving Persia, the last line explained their own situation: subjection to an empire was a lesson in whose servants they really were.
